patient.chief_complaint: Progressive burning pain and numbness in both feet for 3 years
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Garcia is a 64-year-old Hispanic male with a 14-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes who presents to the neurology clinic for evaluation of worsening bilateral foot pain and numbness over the past 3 years. He describes the pain as a constant burning sensation that is most severe at night, interfering with sleep. The numbness began in the tips of his toes and has gradually spread proximally to involve both feet up to the mid-calf bilaterally. He notes that he sometimes cannot feel when he steps on objects and has had two minor foot injuries that he did not notice until his wife pointed them out. He also reports a sensation of walking on sand or pebbles even on flat surfaces. The symptoms are symmetric and have been slowly progressive. He denies any upper extremity symptoms, weakness, or difficulty with balance, though he does note some clumsiness walking on uneven ground at night. He reports his blood sugars have been running high, often in the 250-350 mg/dL range, and he acknowledges poor dietary compliance. He has not had ophthalmologic follow-up in 2 years. He denies any recent viral illness, toxic exposures, new medications, or significant alcohol use. Review of systems is otherwise negative for bowel or bladder dysfunction, recent weight loss, or systemic symptoms.

specialized_test.impression: Moderate-to-severe length-dependent axonal sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy. Sensory nerve amplitudes are more severely reduced than motor; conduction velocities are only mildly reduced proportional to axonal loss with no temporal dispersion and no conduction block. Upper extremity nerves are within normal limits. EMG shows mild chronic denervation distally. Findings are consistent with a length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy

results.finding: 60% reduction in neuropathy with intensive vs conventional insulin therapy

results.finding: Intensive glycemic control modestly slows neuropathy progression

output.summary: Large randomized controlled trials (DCCT, ACCORD) demonstrate that intensive glycemic control reduces the incidence and slows progression of diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Published guidelines recommend annual foot examination with monofilament and vibration testing in patients with diabetes. FDA-approved pharmacologic treatments for painful diabetic neuropathy include duloxetine and pregabalin; gabapentin is widely used off-label. Metformin use is associated with reduced vitamin B12 absorption in population-level studies; periodic B12 monitoring is recommended in this population.

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is a cortical test and is non-contributory in peripheral nerve disease.
Head/brain CT has no role in peripheral neuropathy evaluation.
Brain MRI is not indicated in typical distal symmetric polyneuropathy without CNS signs.
Advanced cerebral imaging (PET/MRA/MRV/perfusion) has no routine role in peripheral neuropathy.
Echocardiography is not indicated unless cardiac amyloid is suspected.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated unless there is syncope or symptomatic dysautonomia with arrhythmia concern.
